items.label: A
items.critique: Short civic-pride lines, a dropped article ('can be dangerous place'), and lore-by-proclamation are pure Nox. Flat, but that flatness is the house voice.

items.label: B
items.critique: Exclamation-driven urgency, plain directions ('just west, down the path'), and a generic heroic thanks ('Your valor knows no peer') read exactly like Westwood's quest-hub guards.

items.label: C
items.critique: Three terse barks escalating to a 'last warning'; jailer humour in one sentence. Could not be more Nox.

items.label: D
items.critique: Stammered 'Wh- who's there?', a nested chain of authority, a burned toll-house backstory and rural titles (the Reeve) pack far more texture into a bark than Nox ever did; the length alone gives it away.

items.label: E
items.critique: Atmospheric and well-made, but semicolon-joined clauses, folk detail ('little lights on the hill') and an English-village register (Reeve, ford, barrow) are not Westwood's plainer, exclamatory style.

items.label: F
items.critique: Dry wit ('He'll take your name and tell you no', 'I may even miss the quiet') is literate in a way Nox's guards are not; three named people and a whole economic backstory in one bark.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Move on!' and 'It's meant for your own good' are stock Nox gatekeeper lines; brief, slightly stiff, functional.

items.label: H
items.critique: 'Greetings!', 'beloved [Place]', 'Delay no longer! The Mayor needs your help!' is Westwood's earnest, exclamation-heavy hero-greeting register.

items.label: I
items.critique: Measured prose with semicolons, 'not a bowshot from here', 'I'll still keep a torch lit, mind' - a novelist's guard. Too long and too textured for a Nox bark.

items.label: J
items.critique: A paragraph of first words with a colon-list, a wry simile ('sooner have back than her own teeth') and a closing quip; far beyond Nox's two-sentence guard.

tells: Length: Westwood's guard barks are one to three short sentences; the new ones open with a full paragraph of backstory.
Punctuation: the new texts lean on semicolons and colons to join clauses; Westwood uses exclamation marks and plain full stops, occasionally ' -- '.

Register: the new texts use an English rural vocabulary (Reeve, ford, barrow, toll-house, bowshot, 'mind') and dialect elisions; Westwood's guards speak generic fantasy-civic ('Greetings!', 'beloved', 'the Mayor needs your help').
Density of names: new barks chain two or three named people and a place per line; Westwood names at most one person and points the player at them.
Humour: Westwood's is blunt and situational ('Don't hassle my prisoners'); the new texts use dry, understated literary wit and closing quips.
The 'later' line: Westwood gives a generic thanks or a new warning; the new texts give a reflective, characterful coda.
